video_caption: The video segment begins with the blue text "OPEN ACCESS," which is then expanded upon with lines connecting to keywords "FREE," "IMMEDIATE," and "ONLINE," subsequently joined by "AVAILABILITY," "RESEARCH ARTICLES," and "RE-USE RIGHTS," all encircled by a light blue cloud-like shape. The scene transitions to the text "This is about making all scientific research content available for anyone anywhere in the world..." (translated: This is about making all scientific research content available for anyone anywhere in the world...) appearing next to an evolving globe that fills with blue and green colors, surrounded by numerous small white papers representing articles, which then fly off to the right. The previous elements shrink and move up as a person with glasses, dark hair tied back, and wearing a blazer, appears on the right, holding papers and looking upwards, accompanied by the speech bubble text "...to read and access and build upon..." (translated: ...to read and access and build upon...). This person is later depicted looking at several papers posted on a wall, with more papers flying in, as another speech bubble states "...so people can do interesting things in new ways with the materials." (translated: ...so people can do interesting things in new ways with the materials.). The scene then shifts to the bottom left, showing two drawn men: one with dark spiky hair holding a clipboard and pen, and another with light hair smiling, while the text "The idea is to make the research literature more" (translated: The idea is to make the research literature more) is displayed. A third man with a beard and glasses then appears between them, smiling and gesturing, and the word "VALUABLE" (translated: VALUABLE) is added in a speech bubble, completing the sentence, with the names "Nick Shockey and Jonathan Eisen" appearing below the three men.

The video segment illustrates the traditional model of scientific publishing. It begins with text on a white background stating, "The History of the model is that publishing scientific manuscripts was...". A man in a hat and trench coat, holding papers, appears on the left, soon joined by another man holding a paper on the right. A dollar sign appears in a speech bubble next to the second man, and the text updates to "...expensive." More figures appear around the first two, all holding papers, as additional text reads, "If you wanted your article distributed widely, you sent it to a journal." The scene then transitions to the right, showing these figures reviewing papers, alongside a man operating a printing press, from which papers are flying out. Another man is seen stacking these printed papers and loading them into a wooden cart or wagon. The text further elaborates: "They would manage the review process, revisions and eventually something would get accepted... and they handled the typesetting and printing and distribution of your scientific work." Finally, the scene clears, and two hourglasses appear around two glowing papers, with the concluding text, "And it worked! Science progressed."

The video segment opens with the text "What's changed is two things:" on the left side of the white background. On the upper right, the text "And it worked! Science progressed" is displayed next to a cartoon hourglass and papers seemingly flying out of it, symbolizing successful scientific progress. At 0:04, the word "Digitization" appears below "What's changed is two things:". Simultaneously, a stream of papers begins to fly towards a central server, indicating information becoming digital. Two individuals are depicted using computers and connected to this server: one person is on a laptop with a thumbs-up emoji above their head, and another sits at a desk using a desktop computer. At 0:13, the phrase "Price Increases" appears on the right side of the screen. Papers are shown flying away from a person with a disappointed expression and a thumbs-down emoji, also seemingly interacting with digital content. Below this, a man in a suit hands a document labeled "bill" to another person, identified as "Librarian," who looks shocked. A thought bubble above the librarian contains a large dollar sign with an exclamation mark, emphasizing the high cost. By 0:21, all these elements – "Digitization," the server, the computer users, "Price Increases," the bill, and the distressed librarian – are shown together, enveloped by a light blue, amorphous background shape. Two additional cartoon characters appear at the bottom of the screen. The character on the right, a man with a beard, has a thought bubble above his head containing the text: "It's become the theater of the absurd with the amount that some journals want libraries to pay." The character on the left, a younger man, is looking at the bearded man, suggesting a conversation or shared concern about the issue.

The video begins with an arrow appearing on a white background, suggesting a timeline, along with two stick figures standing next to a speech bubble that reads: "Research has shown journal prices have outpaced inflation by over 250% over the past thirty years." (Research has shown journal prices have outpaced inflation by over 250% over the past thirty years.) A percentage "68%" is also visible. The scene then transitions to a line graph titled "Price Increases," showing "Journal Unit Cost" rising sharply compared to "Inflation" from 1986 to 2003, with "260%" marked at the peak of the journal cost line, and the "Inflation" line at "68%." The source "Source: Association of Research Libraries" is noted. Below the graph, a stack of books grows, and a speech bubble states: "There are over 15 entire DISCIPLINES where the average prices for ONE journal is over $1000/year." (There are over 15 entire DISCIPLINES where the average prices for ONE journal is over $1000/year.) As more books are added to the stack and colored blue, prices and disciplines like "$4227 CHEMISTRY," "$3649 PHYSICS," "ENGINEERING," "BIOLOGY," "GEO," "BOTANY," "ZOOLOGY," "$1913," "$1689," "MATH + CS," "$1317 GEOGRAPHY," "$2507," "$2281," "$1781," and "AGRICULTURE" appear. Two more stick figures are introduced; one, with a concerned expression, looks at the stack as a speech bubble next to him reads: "Those are just the AVERAGES." (Those are just the AVERAGES.) The other stick figure, with spiky hair, holds a book labeled "TETRAHEDRON" priced at "$40000" as his speech bubble exclaims: "There's a journal called TETAHEDRON that's $40,000!" (There's a journal called TETAHEDRON that's $40,000!) Sources "Library Journal 2012 Periodicals Pricing Survey" and "Robert Darnton/New York Review of Books" are cited, along with "WWW.PHDCOMICS.COM". The scene then shifts to a new layout where the previous graph and book stack shrink to the top left. Several stick figures are depicted amidst scattered papers, representing different roles in academia. One figure in a lab coat (the researcher) says: "The journals aren't producing the material..." (The journals aren't producing the material...), while another (the writer) on a laptop and a third (the reviewer) writing with a pen are introduced with speech bubbles stating: "They don't employ the people who write the papers..." (They don't employ the people who write the papers...) and "They don't even employ the reviewers!" (They don't even employ the reviewers!). Another figure with arms raised (the frustrated academic) has a speech bubble that reads: "It doesn't make sense in terms of what science is supposed to be about." (It doesn't make sense in terms of what science is supposed to be about.) Finally, the raised-arm figure's speech bubble adds: "Science is about discovering new things and spreading that knowledge around!" (Science is about discovering new things and spreading that knowledge around!) The video ends with "CC CREATIVE COMMONS" and "WWW.PHDCOMICS.COM" displayed at the bottom.

The video segment starts with a black and white comic illustrating the scientific publishing system. In the upper left, three cartoon people are shown, two reading papers and one celebrating over a pile of papers. Speech bubbles read, "The journals make money by restricting the information," "They don't employ the people who write the papers...", and "They don't even employ the reviewers!" Below, a government building with many people gathered in front of it is depicted. A speech bubble states, "It's so irrational to think that scientists are paid by taxpayers to do research and distribute it..." A paper falls from the top of the building, landing in a locked box, then a person gives the box with a dollar sign on it to another person, representing payment for access. Speech bubbles here say, "And then, all that work is going to be not made available to people." and "It doesn't make any sense." The scene then transitions to a white background. Next, text appears on a white screen: "This problem of access is something people run into all the time without realizing it." followed by "A lot of people just sort of move on and think, 'Well, this is the way it is.'" and "They don't realize There's a whole system behind it." Three cartoon people are then drawn. One, wearing a cap, sits at a computer looking frustrated, with a speech bubble showing "Access Denied". Another, standing behind him, says "Oh well". The scene then slowly reveals these characters are within a section of a large, brick maze, with papers visible in other walled-off sections. More text appears: "But their education depends on access to the journal literature." and "Professors can only teach what they have access to." An arrow points to another section of the maze where a professor teaches two students from a paper. The maze continues to expand, showing more walled-off areas. Further text appears: "Students and researchers in low and middle income countries really struggle." and "It prevents them from contributing fully to world class research." At the bottom of the maze, two scientists in lab coats stand, looking up at the walls, seemingly outside the restricted areas. Finally, the entire maze structure becomes highlighted in blue, emphasizing its isolating and restrictive nature, before fading to white.

The video begins with a cartoon man with curly hair and a beard, wearing a plaid shirt, explaining in a speech bubble: "Even with this lack of access and even with my brother starting the Public Library of Science… I wasn’t convinced." The scene then shows two men talking, with the first man's sentiment echoed, and the second man asking, "What's the big deal?". The screen then transitions to a dark blue background as the first man narrates a personal story. A speech bubble states, "And then we had a family emergency." A hospital bed appears with a patient (presumably his wife) attached to medical equipment, and another speech bubble states: "I was up at 3am, in the Hospital, next to my wife…" The cartoon man then appears beside the bed, typing on a laptop, with text bubbles narrating: "...surfing the web on the crappy wireless internet... trying to find information about a critical medical treatment... and I couldn't get access to the papers!" A frustrated speech bubble with symbols (#@$%!!) appears from him. The background brightens to a light blue with a heart rate monitor line. Below the hospital scene, the man, now looking distressed with hands on his head, is talking to three medical professionals, while a speech bubble conveys his thoughts: "Our doctors didn't know the answers and we needed to decide what to do. Here I was, a scientist with the ability to understand these papers… And I couldn't get them. That was the moment for me." He then exclaims, "You’ve got to be kidding me!" The screen shows "CC CREATIVE COMMONS" and "WWW.PHDCOMICS". The scene shifts to a white background with text: "Here’s what the problem comes down to in most cases: in that Hospital, I paid." The man is shown typing on his laptop, with multiple "$30" speech bubbles flying out, symbolizing payments for articles. The text changes to: "The problem is you don't know which article is relevant until after you pay for it." The man, frustrated, holds a paper next to an overflowing trash can and exclaims "aargh!". Finally, the text states: "The abstracts don't always make it clear what is contained... and there's no return policy!" The man is shown pointing at a "NO RETURNS" sign while talking to another man, expressing "this is wrong!".

The video segment begins by presenting a cartoon illustration divided into three panels, depicting common problems related to paying for articles. In the left panel, a bearded man in a plaid shirt sits at a laptop, surrounded by thought bubbles containing "$30" several times, with accompanying text, "Here's what the problem comes down to in most cases: in that Hospital, I paid." (meaning: This is the core issue in most scenarios: I had to pay at the hospital). The middle panel shows a man with glasses and a beard holding papers and looking frustrated at an overflowing trash can filled with papers, exclaiming "aargh!" (an expression of frustration), alongside the text, "The problem is you don't know which article is relevant until after you pay for it." (meaning: You discover an article's usefulness only after purchasing it). The right panel portrays a man in a striped shirt holding torn papers and looking distressed, while a woman in a blue top holds a "NO RETURNS" sign. The man says "this is wrong!" and the text below reads, "The abstracts don't always make it clear what is contained... ...and there's no return policy!" (meaning: Summaries often don't reveal enough content, and there's no refund if an article is irrelevant). A large, dark, footprint-like hole then appears in the middle of the screen, with a smaller version of the bearded man from the first panel crawling into it. A speech bubble emerges from the bottom left, asking, "So now are you going to spend $1200 to just find out if possibly they're relevant?" (meaning: Will you pay a significant amount just to check if information is useful?). This is followed by another speech bubble from the right, stating, "If you do that every day, you're in a big hole!" (meaning: Repeatedly doing this will lead to a difficult situation). The scene then transitions to a plain white background with a light blue curved bar at the top and a vertical light blue bar on the right. A drawing of a man with curly hair appears, looking concerned, and text stating, "I'm not a communist." (meaning: I do not advocate for communist ideals). Another man with messy hair joins him, and they sit together on a large sheet of paper. The curly-haired man repeats in a speech bubble, "I'm not a communist." The paper beneath them becomes clearer, displaying "FREE" at the top and "RESEARCH" at the bottom, along with a stylized image of a person with a cap, beard, and raised fist, symbolizing activism. Finally, the text, "Nobody is saying Publishing is FREE." (meaning: No one is claiming that the act of publishing should cost nothing), appears next to the two men.

The video segment presents a comic strip advocating for open access to research. Initially, a partial view shows two men discussing; one states, "I'm not a communist," while the other clarifies, "Nobody is saying Publishing is FREE." Below them is a protest sign with a caricature of a person raising a fist, emblazoned with "FREE RESEARCH." On the right, a speech bubble reads, "But we need to work on models where the government that is already paying for every step..." Below this, a large blue object shaped like a nail, labeled "PUBLISHING" vertically, is positioned before a gradually building brick wall labeled "RESTRICTED" (00:04-00:08), symbolizing the barriers to access. As the wall builds, a Capitol-like building and a crowd of people appear at the bottom left (00:13). Another speech bubble appears (00:15) asking, "Why can't we do it in a way where the knowledge is distributed broadly, and not restricted." Multiple ropes then extend from the crowd and the Capitol building, pulling the "PUBLISHING" object towards the left (00:17-00:19), away from the "RESTRICTED" wall. The word "OPEN" appears in a blue box on the left (00:19). The final shot (00:20) zooms out to reveal the full comic, which includes four upper panels illustrating the problem: a person paying $30 for an article, another frustrated by paying for irrelevant content, a third noting that abstracts are unclear and there's no return policy, and a fourth depicting the prohibitive cost of finding relevant articles daily. The comic is credited to "PHDCOMICS.COM" and "CC CREATIVE COMMONS."

The video opens with the text "There are two components to open access:", which is then spoken by two cartoon men whose heads appear above the text, set against a blue banner. A large light green panel slides in from the left, displaying "FREE to READ" (Free to Read) with three cartoon people below it, holding and reading papers. A darker green panel then slides in from the right, featuring "FREE to Re-USE" (Free to Re-Use) and the explanatory text "Researcher can build new tools that can interact with articles and uncover new relationships." (Researcher can build new tools that can interact with articles and uncover new relationships.). Below this, a grid of 18 empty white squares, representing articles, is shown. The two men from the "FREE to READ" section reappear, one reading a paper, the other a tablet, while a new cartoon man with dark, spiky hair and a blue shirt appears at the bottom right, looking intently at a computer. Dashed lines then connect his computer to the grid of articles, and several squares transform to reveal a green double helix DNA symbol, illustrating the interaction and discovery of new relationships. The scene expands to show four people reading on the light green panel, while the man at the computer now looks frustrated or thoughtful. A speech bubble appears, stating, "Right now, if you wanted to do that, you couldn't, because you'd have to negotiate rights with every single publisher." (Right now, if you wanted to do that, you couldn't, because you'd have to negotiate rights with every single publisher.), and "CC CREATIVE COMMONS" is displayed vertically along the left side of the light green panel.

The video segment displays a static cartoon infographic that illustrates the concept of open access. The image is primarily divided into two large green panels: the left, a lighter green, is titled "FREE to READ" and depicts four cartoon individuals (two men, one woman, one man with glasses) standing and each holding a document, seemingly reading. The right panel, a darker green, is titled "FREE to Re-USE" and features the explanatory text, "Researcher can build new tools that can interact with articles and uncover new relationships," illustrated by a grid of 15 white squares representing articles, some with small tool-like icons, interconnected by dotted lines. Above these panels, a blue strip contains two cartoon men with a speech bubble saying, "There are two components to open access." Below the main green panels, a white section shows two additional cartoon men; the one on the left (with dark, spiky hair) states in a speech bubble, "Right now, if you wanted to do that, you couldn't, because you'd have to negotiate rights with every single publisher," while the man on the right (with lighter hair) looks at a computer screen and says in his speech bubble, "In an Open Access world all this would be free and unrestricted." The bottom left corner of the image includes "CC CREATIVE COMMONS," and the bottom right has the faint text "WWW.PHDCOMICS.COM."

The video segment begins with a light blue speech bubble on a white background displaying the text: "I think the main impediment is the slow movement of scientific cultural practices." (0:00-0:07) Another speech bubble appears below it, stating: "Scientists, despite being great explorers, are very conservative in changing how they do things." (0:07-0:10) A hand-drawn figure in a blue winter coat and boots, holding a pickaxe, is shown pointing forward while standing on a large, white iceberg in water. (0:10-0:15) A second smaller figure, also in winter attire, holding a "NATURE" magazine, crouches behind the first figure. A speech bubble from this second figure says: "A lot of the community says: Yeah, I support Open Access... ...but I want a High-Profile paper." (0:15-0:20) The scene expands to show two more figures on a separate, smaller ice floe, looking up at the iceberg. A speech bubble below them explains: "That sort of reliance on prestige allows some journals to not respond to pressure towards openness." To the right, another person is writing, and a person is being awarded a laurel wreath for their paper, representing traditional publishing recognition. (0:20-0:31) The scene transitions to a white background with the text: "The Scientific Publishing model we have now... There's no evidence it is optimal." (0:31-0:37) A stack of four large, blue, locked boxes, symbolizing restricted access to research, stands on the left, with three people around the bottom box looking frustrated. (0:37-0:38) To the right, the text: "We need to experiment with all sorts of different publishing systems." appears, alongside a stack of open, overflowing boxes with papers, where people are actively engaging with the content, suggesting a more open and collaborative publishing model. (0:38-0:42) The text "Corporations may figure that out before governments do." appears. Below it, a blue cube with circuit board patterns, representing technological innovation, is being worked on by one person with a wrench, while another watches. (0:42-0:46) A speech bubble from the person with the wrench says: "I'm open to whoever is going to come up with creative solutions... I view it as scientists and publishers are slow to change..." (0:46-0:58) Another speech bubble continues: "Some are going to be left in the dirt because Openness is clearly the future... And the creative ones are going to survive." A stylized cow skull appears, symbolizing those left behind. (0:58-1:06) The scene changes to a white background with a text box: "It's really important that grad students start these conversations with their research teams and P.I.'s." (1:06-1:08) Four people are sketched sitting around a table, engaged in conversation. (1:08-1:15) A speech bubble from one of them says: "Let them know this is something you care about." (1:15-1:17) Another speech bubble follows: "There's a real benefit for researchers to do this." Two small papers float down, and two figures are shown below, looking at more papers. A final speech bubble above them states: "The more people that see your work, the more they can build upon it and cite you. It's not just good for the person that can read your paper, it's also good for you." (1:17-1:25)

The video segment displays a hand-drawn comic panel with a white background. In the lower right, a man with a beard and a plaid shirt, seen from the chest up, raises both arms with open hands, exclaiming in a speech bubble, "I believe that science spreads and increases best when there are no restrictions to access." Below him, two other individuals are partially visible: one bearded person in a blue shirt and another with dark hair. In the upper left, two people in blue shirts walk away, and another person in a blue shirt and cap sits, appearing to hold a book, with several sheets of paper floating around them. A partial speech bubble in the upper right corner reads, "for the person that can read your paper, it's also good for you." (This implies that open access benefits both the reader and the author.) The website "WWW.PHDCOMICS.COM" is visible at the bottom right corner of the frame.
